summary: Stone tower on Race Rocks at the Strait of Juan de Fuca, lit in 1860: the Nanette wreck, Davies and Argyle keeper families, and automation in 1997.

structures.note: Scottish granite, assembled 1860 (racerocks); black and white bands. Rowlett dates the tower 1861.
Quarried on the rock; plastered and re-windowed 1873; demolished 1972.
Built to house a fog bell; surf often drowned the bell out.

staffing.note: Resident keepers ended with automation in 1997; Pearson College ecoguardians in residence since 1997.

access.note: Accessible only by boat. Site and tower closed; special permission required to land.

events.note: Site chosen from HMS Plumper's survey on the south side of the outer island; construction 1859-60.
First exhibited 26 December 1860 (Lighthouse Friends); racerocks gives 25 December as the official operating date; Rowlett dates the tower 1861.
Second-order Fresnel lens, shipped from England on the Grecian in August, installed that autumn.
Bark Nanette struck Race Rocks in the days before the light was first shown; cargo sold at auction (Lighthouse Friends).
A boat carrying the keeper's wife's brother and companions capsized near the station, which had no boat.
Keeper George Davies died on the station in December 1866.
Wooden tower built to hold a fog bell.
Keeper's house plastered outside, new windows, doors and steeper roof after Canadian takeover.
Assistant Henry Montrose pulled two deserters from HMS Shah out of the water near the station.
Rowboat of a keeper's son lost in a westerly gale in July 1888; boat found the next morning with one body.
Steam plant and two compressed-air fog horns installed.
Machinery for a three-inch duplicate diaphone plant listed in the Department's 1909-10 works; new fog alarms built at Race Rocks (fiscal 1909-10).
After the Lillooet investigation of the silent zone, the fog horns moved to a separate tower.
Station automated; ecological research station since 1997.
Restored and repainted in time for the 150th anniversary in 2010.

corrections.why: Rowlett lists the Canadian Coast Guard as owner, leased to Pearson College, with Race Rocks Ecological Reserve as site manager. The record's agency comes from one Wikidata entry; a human should check.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Race Rocks was first exhibited 26 December 1860 (Lighthouse Friends) or on the official operating date of 25 December (racerocks). Rowlett dates the tower to 1861. A reprinted Victoria notice in March 1861 still said the light would be shown within weeks; its own date is not given. The story gives 1860 and states the disagreement.

Construction ran through 1859 to 1860 (site chosen in 1859 from HMS Plumper's survey; stones assembled in 1860, lens fitted that autumn). Wikidata gives 1859 and Rowlett gives 1861. The story uses the 1860 completion.

The Nanette struck the rocks on 23 December 1860 (Lighthouse Friends), on the 24th (Victoria Colonist as reprinted in Olympia), or three days before the 25 December operating date (racerocks). The story gives the dates as the sources do.
Lighthouse Friends gives $165,000; racerocks gives an estimated $200,000. The story gives both.

Lighthouse Friends has George Davies moving from Fisgard to Race Rocks to take charge of the first lighting; racerocks has a keeper named Roberts from February 1860 to 1861 and Davies from February 1861. The story names Davies as the keeper who painted the bands and died on the station, and it states the dispute.
Lighthouse Friends gives 1866 and racerocks gives February 1867 for Thomas Argyle's start. Both give 1888 as the end.
Richards's 1859 tracing suggested stone from the island (Lighthouse Friends); the racerocks history says the Admiralty chose Scottish granite shipped as ballast. The story gives both.

Fog bell 1867, steam-plant compressed-air fog horns 1892 (racerocks), diaphone machinery in the 1909-10 works (Marine report). The 1929 Lillooet investigation moved the horns (racerocks). The story gives all four.

notes_for_editor: Checked 2026-10-27 against the cached Lighthouse Friends page, the racerocks history and keeper-list pages, the Lighthouse Directory BC entry, the CCG List of Lights entry G5300, the Washington Standard (29 Dec 1860) and Polynesian (23 Mar 1861) pages, and the corpus tables. Page images read: 1909-10 works table, Changes and Improvements in Existing Aids, printed p. 87 (scan p. 87): Race Rocks has a 3-inch duplicate diaphone plant, $6,800, Canada Fog Signal Co.; the new wooden fog alarm building is at Carmanah. 1907-08 statement of keepers, printed p. 191 (scan p. 200): Race Rocks, F. Eastwood, appointed 21 Jan 1891 per the table (the keeper list says 23 April 1891). OCR-matched by position, not image-checked: the 1911-12 keepers' table (1913v47i15p21_0943, scan p. 81, printed p. 74) F. M. Eastwood. Printed-page footnote for 1907-08 corrected from 'p. 21?' to p. 191. Disagreements stated in the text: first steam fog signal (LF 1881 steam fog alarm vs racerocks 1892 steam plant and horns); Argyle start 1866 (LF) vs 1867 (racerocks); Argyle's pay cut 1880 (LF) vs after 1871 (racerocks); Christmas Eve (LF) vs Christmas Day (racerocks) 1865; the Nanette date 23 Dec (LF), 24 Dec (Colonist via Washington Standard), three days before 25 Dec (racerocks); cargo $165,000 (LF) vs estimated $200,000 (racerocks); keeper's house demolished 1972 (LF, Directory) vs early 1960s (racerocks caption); owner CCG (Directory) vs Pearson College (LF); first keeper: Davies (LF; racerocks keeper list gives Roberts Feb 1860 to 1861, then Davies from 9 Feb 1861). Not in the text but noticed: racerocks gives the light's visibility as 18 miles (1860 context); the List gives a 19 nm range (used). The Directory gives the tower 24.5 m, the List 24.4 m (List used). The 1859 site height (about 8 m / 25 ft above the water) is the Colonist's description of the site, not a tower height. Keepers whose service ended after 1960 are named only in the record above (none named in the story); no personal details beyond the published keeper list. Story has six chapters, all with material: a rich evidence base (annual reports, keeper records, two histories, the List). Wikipedia not cited.
